title: Surat's 'Aqua Garba' Puts Navratri's Dance Moves in the Swimming Pool
excerpt: Youngsters in Surat are performing Garba waist-deep in a swimming pool to Bollywood songs — the latest playful remix of Navratri's most participatory tradition.
body:
• Youngsters in Surat have taken Garba somewhere new: into a swimming pool, performing the traditional steps waist-deep in water to Bollywood songs.
  • Bhaskar English dubs it "Aqua Garba" — the latest in a line of playful Navratri experiments that have included pool dandiya and even an underwater Garba performance.
  • Sharad Navratri 2026 began on October 11 and runs to Dussehra on October 20, so the festive calendar is at full volume right now.
  • Diaspora cue: if your local Garba night feels routine, this is your permission slip — community organizers abroad have run everything from dandiya on roller skates to flash-mob Garba; the tradition survives contact with a swimming pool just fine.

Garba has been performed in courtyards, on streets, in stadiums, and on roller skates. Now add one more venue: the swimming pool. In Surat, a group of youngsters has been performing Garba steps in a pool, water lapping at their waists, moving to the beat of Bollywood songs — a spectacle Bhaskar English has christened "Aqua Garba."

How it works, more or less

Garba's circular, clapping rhythms turn out to be surprisingly pool-compatible. The dancers keep the traditional formations — the revolving circle around the goddess's symbolic center — while the water adds drag, splash, and a fair amount of laughter. It is not a precision performance; that is rather the point. Videos of similar pool dances show participants in festive clothes, unselfconscious and clearly delighted with themselves.

Surat has form here. In 2022, videos of people playing dandiya in a swimming pool in the city went viral, with netizens oscillating between amusement and mock horror. That same year, a group in Udaipur performed Garba in a school swimming pool to Darshan Raval's "Chogada" from Loveyatri, telling ANI it took real dedication to pull off. And India's self-styled "Hydroman," Jaydeep Gohil, took the concept to its logical extreme with an underwater Garba dance, dandiya sticks and all.

Why Navratri keeps reinventing itself

There is a pattern to these experiments. Navratri is among the most participatory of Indian festivals — nine nights of dancing open to anyone who shows up — which makes it unusually remix-friendly. The flaming matka raas of Rajkot, Garba in sunglasses, dandiya on roller skates: each generation finds a way to make the old steps feel like theirs. Aqua Garba is simply this year's entry, arriving right on schedule with Sharad Navratri 2026, which began October 11 and continues through Dussehra on October 20.

The diaspora version

Abroad, Garba nights are often the single biggest community event of the autumn — the Edison expos, the Bay Area grounds, the London halls packed with thousands. They tend toward the traditional, and there is nothing wrong with that. But the Surat swimmers are a reminder that the tradition is sturdier than its purists think. A dandiya night with a twist — a theme, a costume round, a flash-mob opener — doesn't dilute Garba; it does what Garba has always done, which is gather people in a circle and get them moving. The pool is optional. The spirit of invention isn't.
